title: Double-Booking Detector
description: Interval shape on object input — sort depositions by start time, then a single scan comparing each event's start against the furthest end seen so far to surface scheduling conflicts.

reference.approach: Sort by start, scan against furthest end
notes: Sort by start time first — overlap logic only holds once events are in chronological order.
Track the event with the furthest end seen so far, not just the immediately previous one: a long early deposition can overlap several later ones, which a bare `i-1` comparison would miss.
The overlap test is strict — `curr.start < last.end`. Touching boundaries (one ends exactly when the next starts) are NOT a conflict.

questions.q: Why sort the events by start time before scanning for conflicts?
options: Overlap detection compares each event to earlier ones — 'earlier' only means something on a chronologically ordered list
JavaScript requires arrays to be sorted before a for loop
Sorting converts the time strings into Date objects
questions.explain: Conflict detection is about whether an event starts before an earlier one ends. 'Earlier' is only well-defined once the events are sorted by start time.

questions.q: Why compare each event against the event with the FURTHEST end seen so far, rather than just the immediately previous event?
options: It makes the scan run faster
A long early deposition can overlap several later ones; comparing only to the immediately previous event would miss those conflicts
JavaScript cannot compare two array elements directly
Sorting by start guarantees the previous element is always the closest in time
questions.explain: Once sorted by start, the previous element isn't necessarily the one that ends latest. A 9:00–13:00 event overlaps everything starting before 13:00 — you must compare against the furthest-reaching end, not just index i-1.

questions.q: Given `curr` starts after `prev`, what condition means they overlap?
questions.explain: If the later event starts before the earlier one has ended (`curr.start < prev.end`), the two intervals overlap in time.

questions.q: One deposition ends at 11:00 and the next starts at exactly 11:00. Using `curr.start < last.end`, is that a conflict?
options: Yes — they touch, so they collide
No — the test is strict `<`, so a shared boundary is not an overlap
Yes — adjacent events in the sorted array always conflict
Only if the two share the same caseId
questions.explain: `'11:00' < '11:00'` is false, so back-to-back events that merely touch are not flagged. This matches reality: you can finish one deposition and start the next at the same minute.

exercises.prompt: Sort the events by start ascending, grab the first as `last`, and write the overlap test for the next event.

blanks.hint: array method that orders in place
strict comparison — touching boundaries don't conflict

exercises.prompt: Record a conflicting pair, then advance `last` only when the current event reaches further.

blanks.hint: the event that now ends latest

L3.prompt: Given an array of {caseId, start, end} depositions for one attorney, return an array of [caseId, caseId] pairs that overlap in time (the attorney can't be in two places at once).
hints: Sort by start time first, then walk the list once.
Keep a reference to the event with the furthest end so far; compare each new event's start against it.
Overlap is strict: `curr.start < last.end`. Advance `last` when `curr.end > last.end`.
